strengths: Significance: Theorems 4.1 and 5.1 establish a useful way to keep the forward diffusion horizon independent of the desired sampling accuracy. Obtaining a favorable log-Sobolev inequality after OU smoothing avoids imposing this restrictive condition directly on the target distribution.

Originality: Theorem 4.2 provides the most distinctive technical contribution. The score confinement estimate and coordinatewise clipping convert terminal L2 error into exponential-moment control, addressing a genuine obstruction illustrated by the counterexample on page 11.

Soundness: The core decomposition into early-stopping, reverse-process, and initialization errors is coherent and supported by detailed appendices. The discrete analysis supplies explicit complexity bounds and removes a logarithmic accuracy factor relative to the particular baseline analyzed in Section 5.1.

Presentation and ethics: The algorithm, parameter roles, and relationship to existing predictor-corrector methods are explained clearly. Early stopping and the stronger assumptions for discretization are acknowledged. The theoretical analysis and synthetic examples raise no evident material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The headline claim of convergence requiring only L2 accuracy needs qualification. Equations (4.3)–(4.4) retain exponential amplification through the estimator’s one-sided Lipschitz constants. Assumption (A1) does not control these constants across increasingly accurate estimators or as early stopping vanishes. Page 8 introduces an additional stability condition, but its justification is heuristic. Theorem 4.2 also requires separate terminal error control b(T1), which the integrated training loss alone does not guarantee.

The loss formulation does not consistently accommodate singular targets. For a point mass at zero, the likelihood-weighted loss integrated from zero in (3.4)/(4.4) diverges for estimators satisfying the stated global Lipschitz assumption. Equation (4.3) avoids this through positive early stopping. The claimed general convergence consequence should explicitly use a truncated loss and specify the joint limiting conditions.

Some auxiliary mathematical statements require correction. Lemma 4.8’s final KL ≤ d/3 claim fails for d = 1, a point mass at sqrt(2/3), and t = log(sqrt(2)): the KL divergence equals 5/6 − log(2)/2, approximately 0.487 > 1/3. Lemma D.3 also omits the exponential inside its log-expectation, making the literal statement false for exact scores. These appear repairable, but their downstream uses should be checked.

The implementation guarantee has narrower scope than the main continuous-time result. Theorem 5.1 concerns stochastic reversal and requires uniformly Lipschitz true scores, including at time zero; it does not establish a discretized Wasserstein guarantee for the principal deterministic sampler under the broader data assumptions. Additionally, logarithmic dimension dependence applies to the required horizon, while the complete error and complexity bounds retain explicit dimension and Lipschitz factors.

Empirical reproducibility and practical efficiency claims are insufficiently supported. Figure 1 omits the chosen T1, numerical solver settings, network and training details, sample counts, Wasserstein estimation procedure, and error-bar definitions; no code is provided. The three illustrative examples lack comparisons at matched computational budgets and do not evaluate clipping. They therefore support qualitative behavior, but do not establish reduced total training or sampling cost.
